claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering is the primary factor preventing large-scale phase separation in near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing five or more metals.
High configurational entropy reinforces short-range chemical ordering.
Short-range ordering can preserve structural and chemical stability over 473–1923 K under catalytic and thermoelectric conditions.
The proposed initial material is a near-equiatomic, single-phase solid-solution nanoparticle containing at least five metals and having a diameter of approximately 5–10 nm.
Local short-range ordering is present among the constituent metals.
Local short-range ordering produces an enthalpic 'cocktail' effect.
Configurational entropy of mixing enables local enthalpic stabilization of the multicomponent alloy.
Local enthalpic stabilization reduces the driving force for phase separation and rapid elemental segregation as temperature rises.
The nanoparticles will remain predominantly single-phase without major segregation or compositional demixing throughout 473–1923 K.
The nanoparticles will undergo only minimal surface restructuring under reacting conditions.
Comparable binary or ternary nanoparticles, or particles with substantially lower configurational entropy, will segregate or transform at lower temperatures under the same conditions.
Large differences in atomic size can make the proposed stabilization insufficient to prevent phase separation.
A substantial departure from near-equiatomic composition can make the entropic stabilization insufficient to prevent phase separation.
The strength of short-range ordering and the temperature limit of stability vary with particle size and surface chemistry.
The critical threshold for phase changes cannot be fixed without direct measurement.
New XRD phase peaks or significant segregation in compositional maps would show that short-range ordering and configurational entropy did not suffice to maintain solid-solution stability.
